text.p: Swedish automaker Volvo, gearing up for major strategic decisions, has gained a dynamic leader in Electrolux chief executive Leif Johansson but doubts exist over the future of the company's car-making unit.
Johansson, who replaces Soren Gyll at the head of Sweden's best-known company, will bring an innovative approach to Volvo after working for appliance maker Electrolux for 13 years, analysts say.
But the same analysts say Johansson will face some extremely tough decisions, including finding a merger partner to allow Volvo to become big enough to survive among world car makers.
"He (Gyll) led a very successful disposal programme but that programme has been largely finished and they are now entering the second phase of the company after the collapse of the Renault merger.
"This will be a four or five years programme," said analyst Keith Hayes at investment bank Goldman Sachs.
Gyll took power at Volvo after a disastrous and failed marraige with France's Renault.

Johansson immediately opened up the possiblity of seeking merger partners, telling reporters there was little difference between Volvo and Electrolux when it came to examining cooperation possiblities.
"In this type of branch, whether it's cars or white goods, it's natural to look at alliances," he said.
Volvo has been rumoured to be looking at alliance possiblities agreements with Mitsubishi of Japan and Chrysler of the U.S., but no deals in the car units have yet been sealed.
Automotive experts argue Volvo's car unit is too small to survive and that the company needs to get together with a major player.
Gyll said on Monday that his work in changing Volvo into a purely automotive group was virtually completed following the divestment of major subsidiaries.

"Volvo today is strong, financially as well as productwise. The group now faces a number of important strategic and structural decisions that will have consequences extending far into the future," he said.
Gyll said he had intended to retire next year anyway, but -- confirming rumours of boardroom tension in Volvo recently -- he said there had been differences of opinions over strategy.
"You can not change a company of Volvo's size without someone not liking it so much," Gyll said.

Volvo reported pre-tax profit for the first nine months of 1996 of 12.01 billion crowns ($1.7 billion), but this profit -- which included 7.8 billion crowns from a one-off sale of shares -- concealed a sharp downturn in automotive operations.
Automotive profits plunged to 2.16 billion crowns from 6.91 billion for the nine-month period, with the truck division posting a loss. Volvo is due to report its full-year figures on February 19.
The Stockholm bourse reacted calmly to the Volvo change, marking Volvo shares up 1.0 crown.
But in what was seen as criticism of Johansson, Electrolux was marked up sharply, market players welcoming the appointment of Atlas Copco boss Michael Treschow and the departure of Johansson.

Electrolux has struggled in recent years, although most analysts say the problem has been more a question of a flat market for the appliances in which the company specialises rather than any inadequacy of the 45-year-old Swede.
But market players said they would be watching Volvo closely for any signs of strategic change.
"I think investors will look closely to see if they can detect any change in attitude from the management," said analyst John Lawson of Salomon Brothers. ($1=7.243 Swedish Crown)
